speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON INTERNATIONAL SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I referred among other things to a statement made by Lord Home only a few days ago to that effect, namely that these next six months are going to be one of the most difficult and dangerous periods through which we have passed since the last war. I referred to the refusal on the part of the U.S.S.R. to enter into an agreement outlawing the testing of nuclear weapons, to the apparent endeavour of Mr. Khrushchev to emasculate if not destroy the United Nations, and to the threatening if not bellicose statements he has made in recent months.
Coupled with his statement that in the absence of agreement with the west the U.S.S.R. would sign a separate treaty with East Germany and turn over to East Germany control of the access routes to West Berlin, these circumstances taken together reveal the gravity of the situation. Since 1945, there has not been, in the opinion of the leaders of the various free world nations, a situation more serious to contemplate. There is always, of course, the fact that the U.S.S.R. must be deterred from taking precipitate action by the overwhelming fear of nuclear war.
I said further that I felt that the unity of the western alliance, as the Leader of the Opposition has said on more than one occasion, must be strengthened and that, in so far as the nations joined together for freedom are concerned, I hoped they would arrive at a basis of agreement among themselves so that a united stand would be taken and negotiations could continue and be pressed forward, but that negotiation could not be acceptable to the western world if it were to include the acceptance of Soviet abrogation of or unilateral interference with allied rights in West Berlin or the sacrifice of the freedom of the people of that city.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, June 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) for the second reading of Bill No. C-114, respecting the Bank of Canada and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson.

speakeroldname: Mr. M. J. A. Lambert (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a week ago when speaking at the hour of adjournment I had made reference to a document almost six pages long, a letter dated June 26, 1961, appearing over the signature of the governor of the Bank of Canada. At that time I called it a contemptible document deserving only the greatest scorn and condemnation. Those were words of the moment, giving my reaction in the first instance to the spirit and intent of this remarkable letter.
A week's reflection, Mr. Speaker, makes me wonder at the moderation of my language at that time. If he be the true author of this letter, then Governor Coyne has literally taken leave of his senses. He has lost all sense of proportion as between himself as governor of the Bank of Canada, the government and parliament. I will return to this letter later.
Previously I had said that the governor was responsible for the turn of events. He is the one who on June 13 issued a statement to the press when the board of directors was actually considering the matter of his resignation or continuation in office as governor of the bank. This statement which he published had been well prepared in advance, ready for distribution. At that moment Governor Coyne repudiated the responsibility and duty of his office. He was challenging the government; he was entering into the political arena.
This statement was followed by other letters, each progressively worse, not to mention the press conference in the middle of the night. If all this was not cause enough to have the governor sacked, then the letter of June 26 really stripped James Coyne of any vestige of any claim whatsoever to remain at his post. I need not emphasize his breaches of a clear duty when he published confidential memoranda and letters addressed to him or by him as governor of the Bank of Canada.
What has been the public reaction to Mr. Coyne's course of conduct? It has emphasized that the responsibility and supremacy of the elected government in a democracy require that its public servants be seen but not heard on matters of policy except on specific request of the government. The higher the position of the public servant, the more important it is that he should not cross this boundary and transgress on the prerogatives of the elected government which employs him. Perhaps the governor has felt that his position, if one measures it by salary and pension benefits, puts him far above the government. After all, there is a vast difference between his salary and pension and that of a minister of the crown, and indeed even more if compared with the salary and pension

of a member of this house. If Governor Coyne has any such ideas, then indeed he is living in a world of his own far removed from reality.
Now, we know that Governor Coyne did transgress. In months past he has made a number of speeches and pronouncements on Canadian economic difficulties and on economic policy which overstepped the bounds of his office. We have had no evidence at any time, either from himself or from others, that he was ever requested to make such speeches on behalf of the government. In fact ever since May 30, when his resignation was asked for, Mr. Coyne has gone even further in refusing to resign unless forced to do so by an act of parliament.
At this point one may pause and ask why has the governor set himself up against the government? Why has he entered the political arena? Why in fact has he arrogated to himself the functions and duties of a leader of the opposition? His criticisms have been in the same vein and tenor. As a matter of fact there are one or two significant points or questions which arise, and I think we should explore them a little.
First of all, who advised the governor to step over the line and defy the government, yea, even more, parliament, to fire him by an act of parliament? That was a political step which could be motivated, I suggest, sir, only by political considerations. Second, on June 26 there appeared that notorious letter, written in a language and style far removed from that usual with the governor, even those letters of June 9, June 13 and June 16; much more violent, with a good deal of personal invective.
Concurrently, let us recall the debates of June 26 and particularly the speeches by certain members of the official opposition. First of all, the Leader of the Opposition made the request for the appearance of Governor Coyne before the banking and commerce committee. I will not mention the rest of his speech; it was a lot of back room stuff, much of which we have heard in the past in one form or another.
Then we heard from the hon. member for Essex East in his own inimitable style of thunderous indignation, which at times sounds as hollow as are some of his arguments, in which he preached the same message. He was not quite as courteous as the Leader of the Opposition; and we all know, of course, that the hon. member for Essex East feels that he can get as rough as he likes in his posturing and in the booming, sonorous phrases and so on that accompany his speeches on such occasions.
But, Mr. Speaker, we then come to the speech of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, to which I have made reference
Governor of Bank of Canada in another debate. I leave aside any aspect of personal motives because, after all, the rules of conduct in this house preclude me from attributing any malice to the hon. member, and I would not do so; but for pure, unadulterated invective against the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate put on quite a performance. In doing so he may have unwittingly drawn back the curtain at least part way on who has been guiding and advising Mr. Coyne.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is not known for plagiarizing the ideas or statements of others. His mind is quite agile enough both in quality and in quantity to provide him with sufficient ideas for those few times, so he says, when he is on his feet in this house. Let us compare the letter of June 26 and the hon. member's speech of the same day, a speech delivered a strikingly short time after the letter was made public. Let us see what a remarkable parallel of ideas there is between the speech and the letter. Oh, we heard a great deal of talk that there was not going to be any budget, that there was going to be a snap election. We heard about that from the hon. member; we also read about it in the letter.
We heard from the hon. member about the use of a printing press to finance the government's program. We also read about that in the letter. We also heard something, and in this instance I thought the hon. member was treading on dangerous ground, about the quality of the appointments of directors of the Bank of Canada. We also heard read comments about what had happened to the present directors. Unless the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate drew his inspiration from the letter-and I might inquire when he got his first copy of it-then he certainly was most familiar with the thinking of the governor.
I am prepared to go as far as to say that certain members of the official opposition have been consulting with and advising Mr. Coyne in this deplorable affair. We know from his own admissions that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate discussed this matter with the governor in the interval between June 13 and June 26, but I should like to know about the period between May 30 and June 13. Was there consultation? If I have been unfair, and if hon. gentlemen opposite have not been actively advising or consulting with the governor, then certainly it is someone in the hierarchy of the Liberal party, and the pipe line to hon. members opposite is short and direct.
This whole affair, Mr. Speaker, has been a politically inspired move; but would it

Governor of Bank of Canada not be ironic because we know there are many in the Liberal camp who blamed Mr. Coyne for wrongfully advising Mr. Harris in 1957, and who say that as a result of that advice the Liberal party was voted out of office. They had a great love for office, and I am just wondering how far they have been prepared to go to even the score. They could not do anything about it up to now. Oh, some hon. members opposite have done some sniping at the governor, but what a wonderful opportunity was presented after May 30, after a plan that Machiavelli might have admired.

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: Do you mean the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: Are you having fun?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
What about the question of advising Mr. Coyne to take this action? It was obvious to all that Mr. Coyne would have to go, but could they not use the position taken by the governor to berate the Minister of Finance. We know just how much certain members of the opposition love the Minister of Finance, but in order to achieve this end Mr. Coyne would have to go through a political guillotine. But why worry? They had already had too much to do with him. He had harmed the Liberals in 1957, and while retribution might be a little delayed, how certain it was this time. Perhaps Mr. Coyne will wonder whether his head is in a sack because he has been made a dupe for political purposes.
A good deal has been said about the pension matter, which was first raised publicly by Mr. Coyne and was seized upon by the press because of its very nature. The emphasis on this matter is that of Mr. Coyne and his alone. He is the one who upgraded it. The Minister of Finance, who as spokesman for the government has been a welcome contrast to the governor in his restraint in dealing with this matter, has made his personal position clear. Notwithstanding this, the opposition have attacked the Minister of Finance because of Mr. Bryden's resignation. This hue and cry was taken up by Mr. Coyne on June 26, and there again I wonder about the parallel in thinking.
However, Mr. Bryden has made his position quite clear. In a statement on June 28, which has been made public, he has quite clearly set forth just where he stood. He has refuted that canard that he resigned for reasons of disagreement with the Minister of Finance.
I should like to refer to this document and put some of it on the record. Mr. Bryden says that he was first appointed a director of the Bank of Canada on March 1, 1958 for a three-year term. However, in October, 1960 he advised the executive committee that because he was taking an appointment with


the Canadian life insurance officers association in May, 1961, he would have to give up his executive directorship in the bank. He indicated to the Minister of Finance at that time that in the light of this fact it might be desirable to replace him as a director of the Bank of Canada. On the other hand, he was prepared to stay as a director of the Bank of Canada if this might prove possible.

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
May I ask the
hon. member a question? Is he now quoting from the letter of resignation or from the published statement?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
I have referred to the public statement. As of March 1, 1961 Mr. Bryden was reappointed to the board and on March 20 he was re-elected executive director. However, on March 29, 1961, after consultation with his doctor, Mr. Bryden felt it was necessary to retire from the board. The reasons given were included in his letter of resignation which went forward on April 4. The substance of this letter was reported to the house by the Minister of Finance on May 30 in reply to a question by the Leader of the Opposition. Then Mr. Bryden says:
There was some suggestion at that time that these were not the real reasons. I confirmed your statement then and do so again now.
Further down on the same page he says:
Reference has been made by Mr. Coyne in a recent letter to you-
That is June 26.
-that X told you about a possible change in these provisions six months before the directors acted in February 1960. The letter I addressed to you on April 7, 1961 gives in chronological sequence the meetings and discussions relating to both salaries and pensions which led up to the approval by the board of amendments to the pension fund by law. I continue to regard this letter as a confidential communication. At Mr. Coyne's request I subsequently sent a copy of this letter to him in his capacity as governor of the bank, since I was still technically a director of the bank at the date the letter was written.
Here again we have a breach of confidence, Mr. Speaker. Then Mr. Bryden says:
I had two conversations with you with respect to pensions. The first was in August 1959, when in a very casual conversation I said that a subcommittee of the board was giving consideration to the bank's pension fund and to salaries. No reference was made to the special provisions dealing with the pensions of the governor and deputy governor and in fact no details at all were mentioned because, at that time, the board's subcommittee had barely started to work.
The second conversation with you was on March 21, 1961, when X mentioned in another connection, the action taken by the board on February 15, 1960, with regard to the special pension provisions for the governor and deputy governor. You were surprised to learn of this and I was also surprised that you did not know of it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think that will put in a clear light the information that was

made available to the Minister of Finance with regard to this minor affair of the pension of the governor of the Bank of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the issue which is now before the house is a simple one. We are being asked to remove from office one of the half dozen or so public servants in this country who previous parliaments decided should hold office for a term of years during good behaviour. In other words these public servants were not to be removable by the government but only by parliament, and only after misbehaviour had been proven. On June 14, at page 6334 of Hansard, the Leader of the Opposition, recognizing this point, is reported as saying:
The issue before us, Mr. Speaker, is very important but a very simple one. If the government ask parliament to remove the governor of the Bank of Canada because the governor has in fact prevented them from implementing their monetary and financial policies, and if that can be established through a parliamentary inquiry, then, of course,

we on this side would support his removal. That has been the relationship we have put forward all along and we would support it now. That has been the relationship, that has been the doctrine which has been opposed by the government.
The Leader of the Opposition repeated this position when he spoke on second reading of the bill. I should like to put on the record his words which are to be found at page 7054 of Hansard for June 26 of this year. They are as follows:
If the government were convinced that the governor of the bank was really obstructing government policies-and they claim to be convinced now; it is a kind of ex post facto conversion or conviction-parliament, as I have said, should have been fully informed, but it was not informed, and the governor of the Bank of Canada as head of an institution responsible to parliament, should have been given a full opportunity to explain his position and defend it. If he could not or would not explain his position and defend it satisfactorily, then and only then parliament should act.
This, sir, is exactly the position which was taken by a distinguished parliamentarian in this house on August 11, 1956. I should like to put his words on Hansard. They are to be found at page 7458 of Hansard of that date, and I quote:
This parliament, surely, is a court of appeal with respect to any matter, any problem, that lies within the whole scope of federal jurisdiction in this country. Any problem that arises surely ought to be able to find its way for discussion at some time or another on to the floor of the House of Commons. And for my part, Mr. Chairman, I reject completely the doctrine that the Prime Minister enunciated yesterday that parliament has no right to sit as a court of appeal when objection is taken to the exercise by the Bank of Canada of its powers in any particular way. If Canadians feel that those powers have been exercised in any way that they disapprove of, then, surely, this parliament is the forum before which they ought to be able to bring their complaints.
The distinguished parliamentarian who uttered those words was none other than the hon. member for Eglinton, now the Minister of Finance. Far from recognizing that parliament is a court of appeal, as he said it was in 1956, the minister now refuses any information to parliament except that which he gives himself.
In what the minister has told us he has given no evidence whatever of misbehaviour in the legal sense of the term. Surely there is an obligation, there is an onus which lies on the government and on the minister to disprove the statements that have been made. There is an onus on the government to establish misbehaviour. The minister has not stated one single instance, with the possible exception of some unexplained incident in 1957, when the governor of the Bank has failed to perform the duties entrusted to him by parliament, or when he has thwarted government policy.
Governor of Bank of Canada
The minister has indicated that he did not like some of the speeches which were made by Mr. Coyne. None the less he defended Mr. Coyne's right to make those speeches as late as February of this year. What is more, once he spoke to Mr. Coyne about the speeches, Mr. Coyne ceased immediately to make them.
Then the minister said, in a statement that the house has heard, that Mr. Coyne did not possess the confidence of financial institutions by and large. Apparently, he meant the chartered banks of this country. Perhaps the minister thinks the government is responsible to the chartered banks, but we think the minister is responsible to parliament. This parliament has the right to know whether the minister was yielding to pressure from the chartered banks.
These are the questions that parliament, as the court of appeal to which the Minister of Finance referred in 1956, should be allowed to decide after hearing all the evidence. But the minister, who is the accuser, makes himself the court of appeal, and parliament is left to be the executioner.
What is a court of appeal? A court of appeal is one that has all of the evidence before it, the evidence on both sides. A court of appeal is one that hears all the arguments through counsel. A court of appeal is one that has the benefit of the parties appearing before it. If parliament is to be a court of appeal, then parliament is lacking those ingredients which make it a court of appeal. The minister said also that parliament was to be a forum. Where is the forum in this case? Where are the parties who are entitled to be heard? We have heard from but one of these parties.
Then sir, as has already been said but bears repetition, what of the bill of rights? What of the bill of rights that was passed by this government and about which so much has been said concerning the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms? Mr. Speaker, the problem now before the house, stripped of all rhetoric of which, it seems to me, there has been an abundant use, amounts to nothing much after all. It is by reverting to its basic principle that one can determine specifically and objectively what should be the stand taken by the house.
The purpose of the act we are called upon to pass is simply to provide that the office of the governor of the Bank of Canada shall be deemed to have become vacant.
What are the inherent responsibilities of that office and, consequently, what were the duties of the incumbent up to now?
I feel that the first question that should come to our mind is the following: Is the government justified or not in demanding that the monetary policy be subordinate to its economic and fiscal policy?
In my opinion, that is beyond all question. First of all, for a reason of principle that, I think, should be the basis of all discussion and on which everybody seems to agree, namely the sovereignty of parliament.
The government is formed by the parliamentary majority which, in its turn, is elected by the people it represents. Contrary to what has been said, the governor of the Bank of Canada, on the other hand, is an official. Section 7 states:
-is the chief executive officer.
The governor of the Bank of Canada is elected by the directors who are appointed by the governor in council for a term of three years. The election of the governor, whose term of office is seven years, must also be approved by the governor in council. The deputy minister of finance is ex officio a member of the executive committee and of the board of directors but he does not have the right to vote.
The governor of the bank has the power to veto any decision taken by the executive committee or the board of directors but his veto can be disallowed by the governor in council.
What inference should be drawn from the facts recalled and which are the very spirit of this act called the Bank of Canada Act. The inference is, contrary to what we have heard during this debate, that the gover-


nor of the Bank of Canada, as far as his appointment is concerned, as far as his actions and the decisions he is called upon to make within the two boards he presides are concerned, is responsible to the governor in council for all activities within the limits of the powers invested in him.
The fact that the government appoints the directors and, through them, the governor, who is an official, the fact that the deputy minister of finance is a full member of the executive committee as well as of the board of directors, the fact that the governor's veto is subordinate to the approval of the governor in council, all those are legal factors which show that the government has authority over the Bank of Canada and its governor.
This authority should not only be a word; it implies that the government has the duty to define its fiscal and economic policy and that the monetary policy for which the governor is responsible is a consequence of the first and should be subordinate to it.
This is the basic principle neglected by Mr. Coyne, the one he discarded two or three years ago, and this is why of his own free will he has put himself in the position of an outlaw. Finally this is the basic reason why this bill, simple as it is-though full of consequence-should be adopted by the house without hesitation.
Besides, this is in my opinion the principle behind the establishment of that institution, and here I refer to the report of the royal commission following which the Bank of Canada was created, and also to the views expressed by the representatives of the three groups in the House of Commons at that time, in 1934.
First of all, the commission, in its report of 1933, page 63, stipulated as follows:
It Is rather easy to expect too much or too little from the operation of a central bank, which is both an instrument and a force.
As an instrument, it enables the government, with whom supreme authority with regard to money matters necessarily rests, to follow a national policy.
As an authority, the central bank has certain powers which it may use to attain the aims of a national policy.
In other words, the monetary policy of the Bank of Canada must be subordinate to the national policy for which the government is responsible both to parliament and to the people.

What was wrong with replacing their predecessors when their term of office expired? It is the law. It is authorized by the act and because we implemented the act, because, pursuant to that act, we appointed directors we had the right to appoint, here is a man who protests because we caused him to lose his friends, the former directors who surrounded him and who cultivated that spirit

of dictatorship and tyranny which characterizes his letters and his attitudes.
Now, those directors, who are empowered to act, who sit on the board of directors, who have duties to perform, have also told him: "Sir, you must resign".
What does he do? He remains there. He clings to a course of action that constitutes an obstacle to the pursuit of government policy. What is more, he is sowing distrust; by his action, by the stand he is taking, he is sowing the seeds of distrust, he is setting up around the Bank of Canada a wall of distrust which, if this situation is allowed to drag on indefinitely, might be seriously detrimental to that institution.
That is how this man is setting personal interest above public interest. And yet he is relatively well paid to look after public interest.
So, Mr. Speaker, this is the situation in which we find ourselves today. Before closing my remarks, I should simply like to quote an opinion which I think sums up all the others. I should like to refer to an article which appeared three or four days ago in Le Devoir, over the signature of its editor, Mr. Filion, who said in substance: "In the face of the situation in which he finds himself, the only course open to Mr. Coyne is to resign."
For, after all, Mr. Coyne should remember that later on he will not be the one who will have to justify his stand before the people, and to answer for the policies of this government; that will be a responsibility of this government. He has absolutely no responsibility before the people, and yet he would have liked to be heard, yes, and to what purpose? Not to defend himself, as you can see, but to make charges and then attempt to justify these charges. Such is not, thank goodness, the purport of the bill of rights. It is just the reverse, and that is why we could not accept the suggestion put forward by hon. members opposite.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, I say we have here the case of an administrative officer who, for two years, has been advocating fiscal policy, economic policy, financial policy, to the point where one of the documents which he forwarded to us was described even by opposition members, as "the Coyne budget". Can there be any more palpable or concrete evidence of the fact that we are dealing with a man who, constantly overstepping the duties and limitations ascribed to him by law, has endeavoured to lecture the government, to oppose its policies and, in the exercise of his monetary policy, to impede the development programs and the economic and fiscal policy of this government.

Mr. Speaker, is parliament to be denied its own rights and prerogatives which, by the way, are always so eloquently set forth by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) -incidentally, let me say here that I always enjoy listening to him, and he is at his best when reciting the great principles which are the basis of that democracy in which we all share. Well then, I say to him that it is precisely because of those principles, because of the supremacy that the government must enjoy, and of the fact that it will have to give an account of its stewardship to the people of Canada, that a public servant must not exceed his duties, must remain at his assigned station in the hierarchy of administrative functions, and that as soon as he oversteps those bounds and ventures into the field of politics, not only does he violate the obligations he has assumed by reason of his oath, but he acts counter to those fundamental principles that were so eloquently expounded by the hon. member.
That is the reason why this bill is before us. It has been introduced because we want order restored in the household, because we want everybody in his proper place, and because we want no obstacle to stand in the way of the policy for which the government is accountable and which the government wants to translate into action not only through its legislation but by the practical application of that legislation. This is something that requires the unreserved assistance of the country's monetary policy. That is why I feel that the house should, of common accord, support the legislation that is now before us.

We would like to find out the reasons for some of these speeches. We would like to find out also what went on between the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada regarding other matters not touched upon or disclosed in those speeches. We would like to find out what relationship has prevailed in latter days between the directors of the bank and the Minister of Finance. We would like to have from him, in committee where we can crossexamine him as is our right, a statement concerning the propriety of intervening in matters relating to the bank through the intervention of government appointed directors, amongst whom is a former Conservative candidate. These are the things we would like to examine in regard to this matter.
Our attitude toward this bill of attainder- and that is all it is, this bill that recognizes the very opposite that is implicit in the rule of law, in the due process concept in the bill of rights-is that it is a bill we shall vote against for the reasons I am going to explain. The usefulness of the governor of the Bank of Canada has been destroyed by the acts of this government. This is clear. The issue now before us is not whether the governor shall continue in office; that has been established

clearly. The issue is whether he is to be denied the opportunity of acquainting this parliament, through one of its proper instruments, a committee, with his side of the dispute. The issue is whether this parliament is to be denied the opportunity of sifting the facts in a matter so vital to Canada's financial integrity.
It is because in this bill before us, Mr. Speaker, we have a violation of the spirit and letter of the bill of rights that we shall vote against this bill and not because we do not recognize the fact that the Minister of Finance and his colleagues in the government of this country have destroyed the usefulness of the governor of the bank. I would ask the Prime Minister who was not here during the full discussion of this bill, to recall his words last July 1 when the bill of rights was introduced into this house. He said, among other things, that no one shall be denied the right of a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of justice. I ask this house not to forget the words of Professor Scott who, before the bill of rights committee, said that the right to be heard is a principle of natural justice. The right not to be judged by someone who is biased in this case is a principle of natural justice.
We do not deny the right of the Minister of Finance to put forward his side of the case, but we do deny to the Minister of Finance the right to put forward not only his side of the case but that of the man he is accusing, the governor of the Bank of Canada. We want to examine the governor of the Bank of Canada, the Minister of Finance and the directors of the bank so we can find out the particulars of the pension arrangements made for the governor, made by a board of directors the majority of whom are appointees of this government and supporters of this government. We want to know the circumstances because we have grave doubts about certain aspects of that pension and we have not had from the Minister of Finance anything that would satisfy our curiosity in this regard. We are to be denied that right, however, because this Minister of Finance, supporting a government that proposed the bill of rights, says the way justice is to be meted out is by listening to the case of the prosecutor, listening to the prosecutor give the evidence for the accused, and then for the same prosecutor to give final judgement. I would remind the Minister of Finance that justice must not only be done but it also must appear to be done.

It seems to me that the situation before us is this: the minister takes one position, the governor of the bank takes another. Some of us find that some of the facts in this situation are not clear. Some of us have views as to what actually took place. The directors of the bank have a responsibility in this matter, as have the deputy minister of finance and the assistant deputy minister of finance. These men have not been heard. Their point of view has been expressed through a prejudiced party or through a party whose point of view is partisan, the Minister of Finance. We cannot resolve this matter, a matter which touches the vitals of our financial integrity, merely on the say so of a government with a big majority behind it. That is no way to resolve this problem, and no one stated this in principle better than the Prime Minister when he said, as reported at page 5643 of Hansard of July 1, 1960:
-I rise for the purpose of speaking on a subject on which X have spoken through the years,

which has to do with the maintenance and preservation of freedom against governments, however powerful they may be;
That is what is in issue now. This is a powerful government. It has a tremendous majority. Why, then, should it be afraid to test its expression of opinion against those who take issue with it? What has the government to be afraid of?
I have before me the Canadian Bill of Rights, distributed all over this country at the instance of an imaginative organizing body in Bracken house and printed by the Queen's printer. This bill of rights sets out various articles to guarantee that all are given a fair hearing, that there is to be a presumption of innocence, long recognized under our common law. We have at the bottom a statement signed by the Prime Minister. I close what I have to say by repeating what the Prime Minister said, and I ask him to remember these words and to recognize their bearing on the issue now before us:
I am a Canadian, a free Canadian, free to speak without fear, free to worship God in my own way, free to stand for what I think right, free to oppose what I believe wrong, free to choose those who shall govern my country-

speechtext: Hear, hear.

I hope hon. gentlemen will support this, too:
This heritage of freedom I pledge to uphold for myself and mankind.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
After the magnificent and eloquent speech of the hon. Secretary of State it is difficult for anyone to say anything original at this stage of the debate. But all this spurious indignation, the furious and verbose play acting of the hon. gentleman who represents Essex East requires someone to place the issues before the house in perspective, and that I propose to do in a deliberate and, I hope, orderly way. If I succeed, it will certainly be in striking contrast to the contribution made by the hon. member for Essex East, for I say that never in the history of parliament has this House of Commons heard so much fiction uttered in the course of 40 minutes.
The hon. gentleman put up one man of straw after the other, only to knock them down. The greater the falsity of the assertion, the closer the hon. gentleman clasped it to his bosom. The hon. gentleman said the Minister of Finance had threatened to resign. I have been closely associated with the Minister of Finance and I know something of the situation, and I can only say that on the part of the hon. member for Essex East this is but a question of the wish being father to the thought. The hon. gentleman closed his play

acting oration with a quotation from the bill of rights. Oh, I find it touching, this conversion of the hon. gentleman, because I sat in the gallery of the House of Commons in former days when the hon. member for Lake Centre, later the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, and still later the private hon. member for Prince Albert raised this issue on the floor of the house from his seat opposite. The hon. gentleman who is now leader of this government when a private member representing at various times the constituencies referred to raised the question of a Canadian bill of rights, and received from the four horsemen who now sit opposite nothing but scorn. That same hon. gentleman is now the right hon. Prime Minister, the man who a year ago on July 1 triumphed over the scorn of those hon. gentlemen opposite and who placed that great statute upon the statute books of this country. Yes, the hon. member from Essex East would have us believe this afternoon that he has been converted. Well, I do not think the conversion is quite what it was of another Paul on the road to Damascus, but if there be such a conversion in this instance I certainly know there will be some backsliding and probably before the day is out.
Sir, the real issue before this house is a simple and direct one and is capable of only one answer. All the tortuous and incoherent reasoning of the hon. gentleman from Essex East cannot conceal the simple issue. Can a governor, any governor, of the Bank of Canada be continued in office after he has lost the confidence of his board of directors-

That is not the

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: This afternoon the hon. member for Essex East indicated, as he has done on previous occasions, that there cannot be two sovereignties. Of course not. I could not agree more. In fact it is almost the only thing the hon. gentleman said with which I do agree. But what is happening in this House of Commons this afternoon?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: And he quoted that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
What is happening is that this sovereign parliament, the elected representatives of the people, the only sovereign authority, the court of appeal if you
Governor of Bank of Canada like, to use the phrase that the hon. gentleman from Laurier quoted from the Minister of Finance, is being asked to exercise its sovereignty. If the hon. gentleman from Essex East and his colleagues practise what they preach, let them vote for this bill. If they believe that there cannot be two sovereignties, that is the only course they can take. I suggest to them that they desist from the support of a man who with an impropriety never before known in Canadian history uses the full resources of a great national institution, the Bank of Canada, to wage war against the elected representatives, the elected government of the people. Sir, to paraphrase Lord Durham, I say you cannot have two governments warring within the bosom of a single state.
Let hon. gentlemen opposite then support our system of responsible government, not a bureaucratic revolution, for such is the continuing Coyne artillery barrage from his Wellington street bastion. Even Mr. Coyne himself says in the letter which he released on June 26 to the press at least an hour before it was received by its intended recipient, the Minister of Finance:
... an honest difference of opinion proved to be unbridgeable, then it would be the duty of the governor to resign . ..
Can any reasonable man believe that the differences disclosed in this debate are capable of being bridged?

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: Who suggested that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
Surely, after what has transpired, it would be the height of folly to suggest that this government, or indeed any government, and Mr. Coyne could ever work together again. If that be true, sir, then either Mr. Coyne or this government must go. And, sir, it is not our system of government that one bureaucrat can bring down a government. Governments in our nation do not go at the behest of a financier. Only this House of Commons or the people can accomplish the defeat of a responsible government. Can there then be any answer but that Mr. Coyne shall go? In due course this government will submit its record to the people. By that record we on this side are proud to stand and I believe we will survive.
My hon. friends opposite say Mr. Coyne is entitled to be heard. Superficially, sir, the argument perhaps is an appealing one; but it is not one which will stand the test of analysis. Our system of government, as I have said, is responsible government. This means simply that a ministry takes a decision and submits that decision to the will of the elected representatives of the people. By the will

Governor of Bank of Canada of those elected representatives a government lives or dies. And, sir, when the vote comes this government will live.
A confrontation of the government and a public servant, warring within a single camp -such a proposal is totally foreign to our concept of responsible government.
Exalted though Mr. Coyne's position may be, I say that he is entitled to no higher right than any other public servant and no higher right than hon. gentlemen opposite accorded, shall we say, to General McNaugh-ton when they took away his command, or to General Stuart or to Bob Pitt, whose only offence was that he offended the hon. gentleman from Bonavista-Twillingate. This government, sir, believes in one law for all, one law for the exalted and for the humble, not a special situation for Mr. Coyne.
Under our system of government, I repeat, the government takes a stand. It places that stand before the House of Commons. It explains it to the House of Commons, which is its master, and by the decision of that house, and ultimately of the people, a government lives or dies.
But, oh, say my hon. friends opposite, poor Mr. Coyne has had no forum. Well, what do they call the news headlines that this gentleman has created during these past three weeks? Has any Canadian public servant in all of our history ever had the opportunity that Mr. Coyne has had of presenting his side of the case to the public? Is there anything in the world that he could say that he has not said? After all, he has used the complete public relations resources of the Bank of Canada to further his case. How many thousands of dollars of the people's money have been used to further the insurrection of one man who has no backing from his own staff, and who has had the active opposition of his board of directors? These resources have been used to further his insurrection against the elected representatives of the people. Sir, he has not lacked a hearing. He has had every opportunity to be heard up and down and across the land. But my hon. friends say that he stands accused. We have here a situation where they say, "-the bill of rights shall be his protector." I have already indicated what I think of the sudden interest of hon. gentlemen opposite in the bill of rights. It really fascinates me. You would think now when they talk about it today that they had invented it instead of being, when they were in power, members of a government that over the years tried to prevent a bill of rights from being enacted. The bill of rights, sir, was never intended to and does not invade our system of responsible government. This argument about the bill of rights is the

phoniest smokescreen of any that has been raised in this whole debate. I say let us be done with this nonsensical argument.
The only accusations of which I am aware are those which are being hurled constantly from his Wellington street bastion by Mr. Coyne directed at the Minister of Finance. The latest blast which was released on June 26 is so false, so false to my personal knowledge, so biased, so biased to my personal knowledge, so devoid of all principle and common sense that it is unbelieveable that a man in his position could have ever written it.
Mr. Coyne has had many days in which to court the headlines of this country in pursuit of his one objective, namely that of destroying the elected government of Canada. Today that government takes its case to the high court of parliament and it lays its case on the line. Does this House of Commons want Mr. Coyne or does it want this government? Sir, it is as simple as that. No government, Liberal or Progressive Conservative, or any other government that might be elected in Canada, could tolerate any type of insurrection no matter how exalted maj be the insurrectionist.
The unhappiest fact of all is that hon. gentlemen opposite are seeking to exploit this incident for purely political purposes. They seek to exploit the defiance of government policy by the governor of the Bank of Canada, his equal defiance of his own board of directors, his defiance of leading Canadian businessmen on the board of directors drawn from every province of Canada and from every walk of life. I say to this house with great seriousness that hon. gentlemen opposite have shown a very scant regard for the future, for the integrity, the independence of a great national institution, the Bank of Canada.
To me, sir, the most deeply regretted situation of all this whole Coyne controversy has been the willingness of the governor to make a political football out of the institution to which he has devoted most of his mature life, or perhaps I should say his adult life, and of which he has been the directing head for 6J years. I include in that regret the present utter impropriety in using the great resources and public relations facilities of the central bank to foster a political dispute.
It has been the governor who has shown a reckless disregard of the consequences to an important national institution. It has been the Minister of Finance and the government who have demonstrated patience, consideration, dignity and statesmanship. In true Louis XIV style the governor has adopted the attitude, "La banque, c'est moi". He has

shown a determination that if down he goes, as down now he must go, he will pull down with him the institution that gave him his opportunity and which is of such vital importance to Canada.
What has happened to his judgment is something that I simply cannot understand. Hon. gentlemen opposite need no words of mine to convince them of the intransigence of James E. Coyne. Members on the front bench opposite are not unaware of the fact that the present Minister of Finance is not the first minister of finance to find Mr. Coyne difficult, brooding and unco-operative. But, sir, what is most important is the fact that all except the most purely formal relations between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the financial community had come to an end. There has been almost a total breach between Mr. Coyne and the banking and other financial institutions of this country. Is everyone out of step except Mr. Coyne?
The hon. member for Essex East tried this afternoon to suggest that in some way there had been a conspiracy. He tried to arouse suspicion. I say to him that this is not worthy, that that is not in fact the situation. What has happened has not been a case of bogeymen of evil financiers who have been attacking Mr. Coyne. What has existed has been a total incompatibility of personal relations, a brooding, moody, ivory-tower attitude on the part of the governor, one man lonely in his majesty, one man against all the economists of government and financial institutions and, as we saw last autumn, against practically all the economists of the universities.
As this situation became increasingly apparent, as the governor more and more recklessly involved the Bank of Canada in political controversy, as increasing evidence mounted that our economy was suffering from the stubborn refusal of the governor to adopt flexible policies needed to give the economy a renewed stimulus, what was the government to do? It could have stood back until December 31 and merely let the whole sorry Coyne era disappear into an unlamented and unmourned past. It could have exercised a further restraint. It could have exercised a patience already severely taxed. Certainly that would have been the easy way. What it did was to act honourably. What it did was to tell Mr. Coyne that his term would not be renewed, that there were only 6J months to run and that he stood in the way of the implementation of a comprehensive, sound and responsible economic program designed to raise levels of employment and production in Canada. This is what Mr. Coyne sought to prejudge and to prejudice in the public mind by a blast in which he
Governor of Bank of Canada described it as "mysterious and alarming". We may test what he has to say by this comment. Do any other Canadians consider the budget "mysterious and alarming"?
Mr. Coyne decided, as I have said, that he was greater than the government, that his personal future was more important than that of the Bank of Canada, and he declared war on the government and sought to bring it down. Not for a moment, sir, do I deny Mr. Coyne's right as a citizen to resign and to campaign to the limit against the government but I do dispute most vigorously the right of any servant of the crown to remain in office and to declare war on Her Majesty's ministers who have the confidence of this House of Commons, and to use the full resources of a great crown agency to fight his personal battle. I say that in all the history of parliamentary government I know of no counterpart of the utter impropriety of Mr. Coyne's actions, of his total disregard of the principles upon which responsible government is based. Let him step aside and use his own not inconsiderable resources and not the Bank of Canada's resources to fight his personal battle.
In my view what is now the most important aspect of this whole issue is to have appointed a new governor as soon as possible whose high qualities will command the confidence of the public and the business community alike.
From the recital of events given to the house last week by the Minister of Finance, it is abundantly clear that the Minister of Finance and the government have been running interference for Mr. Coyne for at least three years, endeavouring to protect him from the consequences of his own folly and, as it now appears, from the advice he was receiving from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. They were protecting him despite the fact that he was persisting in public utterances at variance with, indeed almost in defiance of, government policy, that his utterances were entirely outside the field of monetary policy and were entrenching entirely upon matters within the exclusive prerogatives of the government, that he was embroiling the Bank of Canada in political controversy, that he was becoming increasingly at loggerheads, as I have said, with the whole financial community with whom the national interest required that he work on a day to day basis of mutual trust and confidence. Small thanks indeed have the Minister of Finance and the government received from Mr. Coyne and his political commissar opposite, the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, for the protection accorded to him sometimes in acutely embarrassing situations.

Governor of Bank of Canada
The last letter addressed by the governor of the Bank of Canada to the Minister of Finance, dated June 26 but, it is to be noted, released on that day by every Bank of Canada office in every part of Canada, is the most outrageous and unprincipled document I have ever read. The recklessness of his charges, the baselessness of his conjectures and diatribes, the lurid, hysterical language, were described by one newspaper as equalling a paper-back mystery thriller. I doubt the comparison for I have never read such a thriller which so completely departed from reality.
He states categorically that "the budget was rewritten after my statement". From personal knowledge I know that not to be the case. Yes, of course, editorial changes are always made in a budget up to perhaps 48 hours before its delivery but as to the main principles of this last budget they had been fully settled before Mr. Coyne was asked to resign and remained unchanged thereafter.
Words like "blackmail", "subversion", "ulterior", "political puppets", "degraded" abound in this letter which is as atrocious in its bad taste as it is in its utter falsity. He says in this letter that he was warned of a certain danger "by a man whose opinions I value". Hon. members who have sat in the House of Commons with him do not quite share Mr. Coyne's evaluation of the opinions of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate.
It is the role of the government and of parliament to govern. Majority rule in this House of Commons must not be frustrated, I say, by opposition infiltration into sensitive public service areas, seeking to set at nought government policy. I say, let the elected representatives govern, not some invisible and irresponsible group headed by the grey eminence from Bonavista-Twillingate.
Quite a bit has been said about the pension aspects of this whole matter. This is but an incident, the fifth and last matter mentioned by the Minister of Finance in his discussion on May 30. Yet, so sensitive was Mr. Coyne that he tried to boil it into the principal issue. Sensitive-yes, but methinks the laddie doth protest too much.
In so far as my farmers and civil servants in Carleton are concerned, $25,000 a year is a lot of pension for a man of 50. However, I suppose it is nice if you can get it. This needs to be said, sir: Mr. Coyne at age 50 wants more for not working-for not working, mark you-than we pay the puisne judges of the Supreme Court of Canada for working until age 75. We pay the judges of that court $22,500 for working to age 75 and yet Mr. Coyne wants $2,500 more for not

working at age 50. The governor of the Bank of Canada is a very important officer, but the people of this country have a high appreciation of our Supreme Court of Canada. We pay the deputy minister of finance, a most important official, $23,000 for working until 65, but Mr. Coyne wants $2,000 more for not working at age 50. There must be some sense of proportion, some relativity, and it is immaterial to me what the directors approved. I say only that I am ready to face my electors of Carleton at any time on my view in respect of this particular matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR

So, the hon. gentleman says no. He is now in the clear with his Sifton friends. In order to adopt this particular proposal, we would not only have to denounce GATT but we would have to denounce every trade treaty that this country has entered into under a Liberal government or a Progressive Conservative government. Should we denounce our treaties with the United Kingdom, with the United States, with Australia, and stand alone in the world? Mr. Coyne would have us in a position of magnificent isolation. Not only would we have to denounce our trade treaties, but Mr. Coyne would have us denounce all our tax conventions, terminate all agreements in respect of non-resident withholding taxes and raise the rate to 30 per cent. My hon. friend says, "and without a hearing".
Canada has never had the reputation of being a treaty breaker. I doubt if the country will go along with Mr. Coyne or any of his Liberal allies opposite and give them the opportunity to blacken our international name. Hon. gentlemen opposite, in the budget debate and since, have asserted that tax reductions are a desirable stimulus in times of economic slowdown. What does their erstwhile comrade in arms, Mr. Coyne, say? He advocates an immediate 3 per cent increase in the corporate and income tax. Do my hon. friends adopt that policy? Once you submit the whole of Mr. Coyne's memorandum to critical analysis of this type, you find that obviously it is not all bad and equally obviously it has many features which are totally impractical, some actually mischievous, some so harebrained that it is almost impossible to believe the memorandum was composed by a man who has spent a large part of his life in the field of economics.

I am afraid, sir, that those who read this memorandum carefully and reflect upon its proposals will have portrayed more vividly than any words of mine the problems endured by the Minister of Finance in endeavouring to deal with this governor. Governor of Bank of Canada allowances would be reduced, if not done away with. Regrettable and damaging, sir, would be the consequences to many communities in various parts of Canada.
Mr. Coyne's memorandum displays what I might describe as his morbid dislike, almost hatred, of foreigners. This has permeated all his advice to the government. His recklessness in this respect would lead Canada to the brink of disaster. One might go on examining this fantastic memorandum. I only repeat that out of his own mouth is he condemned. The quality of the advice which he is capable of tendering to any government is here exposed for all to see.
Hon. gentlemen opposite naturally seek to defeat this government. That is their right, indeed that is their obligation and that is the democratic way. What I am totally unable to comprehend, however, is how they can give their support to an attempted coup, a coup d'etat, whereby one public servant, violating every principle and ideal of the public service, seeks to bring down the government and usurp the role of this House of Commons. This is not the Canadian way.

Well, sir, if there is one principle that matters, in my view it is the maintenance and preservation of the integrity of the Bank of Canada in the image which Graham Towers gave it. With an utter disregard for consequences, Mr. Coyne suggested that a new governor would be subverted and his ghostwriter in this house apparently said the new governor would be a "stooge". I say, sir, that words like that work a grave national disservice. Let us all remember that Canada is much greater than any one of us; that all of us will pass from this scene but hope we will leave Canada stronger and more united.
This I know: No man will be appointed to the role of governor of the Bank of Canada by this government who is not a strong, vigorous and experienced person capable of giving to the Bank of Canada real and effective leadership, leadership of the type which

Governor of Bank of Canada has been denied to it in these last years. This government believes in the significant role of the Bank of Canada, and as soon as this parliament disposes of Mr. Coyne, that bank will be placed in the soundest position in which it has been since the days of Graham Towers. To that end, I suggest we direct all our efforts.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary secretary rose, he said, to set the issues in perspective. If that was his purpose, he has failed miserably. He sought to erect a straw man out of tangential issues and has completely ignored the two overriding ones. They are first, fundamental justice, the right of the accused to be heard; and second, government responsibility. The parliamentary secretary said our system is responsible government. May I say that there is nothing responsible about this government. In this case it might be more accurate to say a government lack of responsibility, a government which has never been big enough to take responsibility for the unpleasant. Of course, when things go well, it is thanks to government intervention, but when things go badly, it is the fault of someone else.

speechtext:
First after the government was elected the scapegoat was the Liberals; it was the legacy they were left. Then it was external influences beyond their control, they said, which kept them from running the Canadian economy properly. Now at last it is the governor of the Bank of Canada. Again the government refuses to accept its responsibility and has looked for a scapegoat. It is this insistence on always finding a scapegoat which is so objectionable, Mr. Speaker. This attitude of the government reminds me of a quotation from Morrow:
Any party which takes credit for the rain must not be surprised if its opponents blame it for the drought.
The truth is, Mr. Speaker, that the government has got itself into a box and has chosen a cheap and, as it hopes, an easy way

to lay this blame on the shoulders of someone else. The government has been in constant trouble. The evidence is everywhere. There have been many reports. Here is just a sample. This appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of January 6, 1961 in an article by Mr. Jack McArthur, the financial editor.
I quote it in part:
Painted into a Corner
Here's where it gets funny.
Mr. Fleming, although he apparently would like to reduce interest rates, has painted himself into
a corner.
He has said often and loudly that money policy is a responsibility of the Bank of Canada-and that the federal government has no control over the bank.
He has not even been willing to comment on the central bank's money supply and interest policies.
How can he possibly now try to persuade the Bank of Canada to listen to him? So he and. the government must try to run their own private interest rate policy and pretend the Bank of Canada isn't there.
If that isn't good for a real laugh-and a few tears-then nothing is.
Having been painted into a corner, what is the government to do? The depth of the desperation is shown very clearly by simply comparing the statements of the Minister of Finance in this year's budget with those of last year. This year he proposes as visionary that which last year he said was impossible. One example which has been stated in this house is that of manipulation of the foreign exchange fund. Whereas a year ago he said that it was a speculation with no assurance of success, this year he says rather than by direct government controls, subsidies, quotas or tariffs he would undertake a manipulation which would bring down the exchange rate by indirect methods. Precisely, however, a year ago he said this type of thing would likely lead to direct controls. Now he has made a right angle turn.
This raises a very fundamental question. I was interested in listening to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) this morning. He also seems to be a recent convert. At noon I was reading in Hansard a statement of his where a new policy was being embarked on, and he insisted that the governor of the Bank of Canada be brought to a committee to discuss the issue, that this was in all fairness the only way in which it could be dealt with. Today he takes an entirely different attitude. I remember also, in that same committee at the time the bank act was revised, the hon. gentleman's insisting that some limitation be put on the power of the Bank of Canada to increase the money supply. He it was who feared an irresponsible government. He it was who feared the possibility of some future government starting the printing presses and going into a wild inflation of the Canadian currency. What has happened

in the intervening years to change his mind? Was he more visionary then than now? Or was it simply that he could foresee at that time a government of the calibre and lack of responsibility of the present government?

The other fundamental question, Mr. Speaker, is that of fundamental justice. The governor of the bank has been accused of obstructing government policy. The supporting evidence has not been produced. How can this procedure be squared with the bill of rights? I recall July 1, 1960, bill of rights day. The Prime Minister was at his best. The Prime Minister was most eloquent. How our hearts beat with pride and with joy on this great date of bringing in a new era of rights and freedoms for the average Canadian citizen.

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR

To their shame they now
applaud tyranny. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Revenue cited

Governor of Bank of Canada a strange doctrine today. If we gave the governor of the Bank of Canada a chance to be heard, he said we would then have to give the same right to every other government employee, to every clerk. What a red herring that is, Mr. Speaker. Civil servants are employees of the government and they have a right of appeal. The governor of the bank, on the other hand, is responsible to the parliament of Canada. If the government wishes to introduce an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act in order to change the relationship between the governor and the government, it has the right to do so. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but if it believes it should be done, it has the responsibility to do so. Many people have made this suggestion. speechtext: He has not behaved well.

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance has not made any categorical accusation of misbehaviour. The accusations are by innuendo; the charges are by inference. If parliament passes this law without hearing the evidence it will be flouting two of its own laws. It will by inference have accused a man of misbehaviour and found him guilty without giving him the benefit of trial. It will also flagrantly disregard the bill of rights, which explicitly denies a statute taking away rights and freedoms which had existed long before the fair weather champions opposite chose to espouse them.
The Secretary of State has stated in his loudest voice that the issue before us today is the issue of the supremacy of parliament. That is not the real issue, Mr. Speaker. There is no question about the supremacy of parliament. The real issue-and it is the same issue embodied in the bill of rights-is the duty and responsibility of parliament not to pass laws taking away from the individual the fundamental right to a fair hearing.
I must oppose this procedure, Mr. Speaker, because I must stand on the principle of the right of a free man to be heard before the court that condemns him.

Have the markets changed or altered somewhat? Will the products to be shipped by Hudson Bay Oil and Gas Company and by Aurora Pipe Line Company as is contemplated be sent to markets somewhere else? Has there been an alteration? I think these are very important questions especially in view of the desire of everyone in the house to promote the development of industry in Canada.

I certainly want to co-operate in every way and I can only say that when my good friend from Macleod had another bill with reference to a railway line before the house he pointed out that the same by-products were being exported to the United States. Condensate, of course, is a high form of crude petroleum. As I pointed out, it is a surplus commodity in the province of Alberta and it is a case of exporting it. The fact is that we have a surplus in the province of Alberta. The hon. member for Skeena will appreciate that those are the points that will come before the national energy board and will be ironed out at that time on the basis of proper evidence. There is no doubt that if this pipe line is allowed to proceed export will be to a different part of the United States from that mentioned earlier. This is a surplus commodity. It is a by-product of natural gas. As I pointed out on a previous occasion, we have a reserve in the province of Alberta of some 23 trillion cubic feet and the demand in Canada, even

projecting, would amount to about only 10 billion cubic feet per year. It is a surplus commodity as are beef from the foothills of the Rockies and wheat as I have said on previous occasions. It is a commodity to be exported by a pipe line. As I pointed out on previous occasions, in order to export it across an interprovincial or international border it is necessary to form a special company. That was why Hudson Bay Oil and Gas came here to parliament. As a matter of law, we had to come to parliament to ask for incorporation.

When that gas is processed some of the by-products will be ethane, methane, propane, butane and hydrogen sulphide. Certain of these by-products are a drug on the market. speechtext: I wish to assure the committee that I intend to take only half a minute. However, I feel that it is a bit of a contempt of parliament for the Alberta energy board to have taken the measures it has taken and also for the cabinet of the government of Alberta to have taken the measures it has taken in this regard before allowing the parliament of Canada to reach a decision. They have given all the rights to the parent company even though, I will admit, they have not dealt with the Aurora Pipe Line Company as such. However, they were completely aware of the implications of their actions. They were also aware of the fact that this matter was before the House of Commons at the time they made their decision. I do not know whether there is any proper procedure but I would say that the Alberta energy board and the Alberta government are guilty of being in contempt of this House of Commons because they took action which completely nullified any decision that we may make either one way or the other.

subtopic: AURORA PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I should like to follow along with that line of reasoning very briefly, Mr. Chairman. You will recall that, at previous stages of discussion of this bill, numerous arguments were made that what parliament should do is merely to pass the bill without question or discussion because we have a national energy board, because it was established by parliament because it had certain functions and responsibilities and so on. It was argued that we should therefore entirely give up the right to make a determination of these matters to a board which has been established by parliament.
As you will know, Mr. Chairman, we objected to that line of reasoning as not being valid. What the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has just said, in my opinion, has even more force than our argument previously

because the board that made the decision in this regard is not a board that has any responsibility to the parliament of Canada. It is one established by the legislative assembly of the province of Alberta and the provincial government is involved in that particular decision.
It is true, of course, that the government of Alberta cannot grant licences for or deal with exportation to another country or to another province. Here the national energy board comes into the picture. However, I think the Alberta gas and oil conservation board is perhaps not entirely to blame in this regard, but rather that Hudson Bay Oil and Gas Company has acted a bit contemptuously also, knowing full well that as the promoter or parent company of Aurora Pipe Line Company, it had applied or petitioned for a private bill to establish this company. Hudson Bay Oil and Gas Company also knew full well that the matter had not been dealt with by parliament. Yet at the same time as this legislative action was not completed it proceeded, as I say in a contemptuous way for the feelings of parliament, to make applications and to process those applications before the Alberta conservation board, without having any statutory approval of the particular company which it was fostering and promoting.
It is a bit contemptuous of and a bit of an affront to parliament for a private company so to petition, to plead and to argue for the establishment or the incorporation of a certain company to do certain things and then, without regard to what decision parliament might make, to proceed on its own hook to get authority from other sources to do some of the things with which Aurora Pipe Line Company will be connected.
It would seem to me that parliament should concern itself more with the activities of private companies, especially those controlled in the United States, as is Hudson Bay Oil and Gas Company and as this company will be. Parliament should concern itself with the activities of those companies especially when they are handled in this particular manner, especially when a petition is made to incorporate a particular company because the law requires it-that is to say, the National Energy Board Act requires it-and then by the back door they go somewhere else and proceed just as if parliament had endorsed and authorized the establishment of this particular company.
On that basis alone I would be inclined to object to the passage of the bill and to vote against it regardless of the merits that exist for voting against it in the field of international control. I think it should not go unnoticed that Hudson Bay Oil and Gas

Company have acted in this way, as is probably typical of companies of this type controlled by what the Prime Minister referred to, generously or ungenerously, as Texas buccaneers. I think that this is an indication of the manner in which they are wont to operate and I do not think that parliament should let it go unnoticed.
