speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
We are now in committee stage on this short but very important bill which deals with the office of the governor of the Bank of Canada and which states that it shall be deemed to have become vacant "immediately upon the coming into force of this act". That is all, but that is a lot.
In the first place, I should like to point out, in contradiction to some of the things which were said about this office of governor this afternoon, that the governor of the Bank of Canada is not a civil servant. A lot of the argument which was based on that this afternoon has, of course, no validity at all. I should also like to point out that this bill, in a sense, though in a very wrong sense, does represent an acceptance by the government of some responsibility, if not for monetary policy, then at least for the governor of the Bank of Canada. This afternoon we heard an extraordinary statement from the Secretary of State-extraordinary in relation to the statements we have heard from the Minister of Finance-that the government does, indeed, have responsibility for monetary policy and, in that sense, for the governor of the Bank of Canada whose office is to be vacated as a result of this bill. I say this was a most extraordinary statement because it has been denied vehemently and repeatedly by the Minister of Finance. Perhaps those two ministers might get together in the interest of cabinet solidarity and decide what is the position of the government in this vital matter.
In committee we can ask some questions. I know this is a procedure which is deprecated by the hon. member for Edmonton West who objected to having this matter sent to a committee-not, of course, to the committee of the whole, but to a committee-because it would mean that "the bully boys of the Liberal party," which I think was the expression he used, would ask questions. To him it was a terrible thing that the masses

of Tories in committee were going to be overridden by the bully boys in the Liberal party, so little confidence has he, apparently, in the ability of the majority to take care of itself.
We are in committee now. I can assure the hon. member for Edmonton West we have no Machiavellian purpose in the questioning we intend to put to the minister. As a matter of fact, the hon. member carried Machiavellianism to absurd lengths this afternoon when he said this whole business which is now before us, this bill in committee, was nothing less than a subtle plot on the part of the Liberals to get rid of Mr. Coyne. That is a new interpretation of this issue. Mr. Coyne offended us, presumably, in the elections of 1957 and 1958 so we are getting rid of Mr. Coyne by luring him into this situation. That, Mr. Chairman, is something very new indeed, and in its absurdity it is only equalled by some of the statements the hon. member for Carleton made this afternoon.
On March 21, 1957, the hon. member for Eglinton-he was not then minister of finance -had this to say as reported in Hansard at page 2557:
-the Minister of Finance, so far as we are concerned-
He is speaking of the minister of finance of that day. The hon. member was talking about the Bank of Canada matters.
-is not going to hide behind the policy of the Bank of Canada. He is going to bear his own responsibility.
Well, the present Minister of Finance is going to bear his own responsibility in this matter today and we intend to examine him on this very short bill in a way which I hope will elicit or bring to light some of the issues in this matter which have not been brought to light so far, so that we may be enlightened with regard to some matters about which we have only had partial, subjective and prejudiced evidence. We are, of course, within our rights in cross-examining the minister on all aspects of this bill which is designed to vacate the office of the governor of the Bank of Canada. It would, of course, have been much easier, much more effective in every way, besides being fairer to the government and to the governor of the Bank of Canada if this matter could have been submitted to the kind of committee where all those concerned might have been questioned. That is not possible, but we have at least the opportunity in committee of the whole to question the minister himself. The minister will not, of course, object to that, because he himself invited it, and in order to anticipate any difficulty which might conceivably arise in the hours ahead I should like to put on record the
Governor of Bank of Canada words of the minister on this point as reported at page 7096 of Hansard of June 26. The hon. member for Timmins was speaking, and had this to say:
The Minister of Finance said that parliament must decide, but we must decide in the dark; we must decide blindly; we must decide just on the statement of the minister. We are not allowed even to get the minister before a committee where he can be cross-examined.
Then the minister replied:
Yes; you will have the committee of the whole after second reading-
For cross-examination, and that, of course, Mr. Chairman, is what we propose to do.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
It is, of course, a one-sided examination but we shall do the best we can with it in the absence of other witnesses who might be able to throw some light on these matters.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this matter was first brought into the House of Commons on June 14 as found at page 6326 of Hansard. The Minister of Justice intervened at that time and had this to say:
Legislation to amend the Bank of Canada Act itself will be introduced shortly.
That was a plain and categorical statement but like so many statements which come from hon. members on the treasury benches, it had no foundation whatever in fact because this is not legislation to amend the Bank of Canada Act which the Minister of Justice said would be introduced shortly. It
7512	HOUSE OF
Governor of Bank of Canada is not even legislation which had been introduced shortly. If the government had been anxious to clear up this matter quickly they would have introduced this legislation at once; they would have allowed it to go before a committee. It could have been dealt with in committee; it could have been brought up and dealt with on third reading and the matter would have been cleared up one way or the other. That was not done. It has been allowed to drag on. On June 14 the Minister of Justice said that legislation to amend the Bank of Canada Act itself would be introduced shortly. We have not got that, and apparently there was never an attempt to do that. That was just an argument made by the Minister of Justice. The legislation we have is merely this:
The office of governor of the Bank of Canada shall be deemed to have become vacant immediately upon the coming into force of this act.
I repeat "shall be deemed to have become vacant". This is an office not of a civil servant but of a high public official appointed not at pleasure but for good conduct, which office will be deemed to have become vacant by an act of parliament, if it is passed by parliament.
There are lawyers who have already said that an office which has been vacated in this way by an act of parliament can be filled only by an act of parliament. I leave the lawyers to argue that and perhaps we shall have some argument on it before the evening is over. But I ask the government and the minister why the Bank of Canada Act itself was not amended to deal with this matter, as the Minister of Justice said it would be? Why was it done in this way? If this crisis had to arise-and it did not have to arise but the government assured that it did arise-if this situation had to be dealt with by legislation -and the government again assured that it had to be dealt with by legislation-why was not advantage taken of this unhappy opportunity to amend the Bank of Canada Act so that a situation of this kind could not arise in the future? That was not done. The government preferred to operate in this other way.
Why was our Bank of Canada Act not brought into conformity with the bank of England act under which a situation of this kind could not arise? There the minister of finance, or the chancellor of the exchequer, who is responsible in this area of policy, may, in a dispute with the governor of the bank of England, impose his views on the government of the day on monetary policy in writing, and if the governor of the bank of England disagrees and there is no way of resolving that disagreement, he resigns in 

writing and his resignation can become the subject of public and parliamentary information and discussion.
In this situation the responsibility for monetary policy is firmly fixed on the government, as the Secretary of State said this afternoon it should be fixed on the government, and as the Minister of Finance said yesterday it was not fixed on the government. The governor of the Bank of Canada who is being thrown out of his jobs by this bill without a hearing before the parliament which is throwing him out of his job has written, "the bank"-that is, the Bank of Canada- "must take into consideration any views on monetary policy expressed by the government and in the event of a sufficiently serious difference of opinion on a matter of an important point of policy it would be the duty of the governor to resign". That, of course, is a doctrine we accepted long before the present government paid even lip service to it, but in this case, Mr. Chairman, the governor of the Bank of Canada denied that there is the kind of dispute that justifies this type of legislation. He asks for evidence to refute the statements he has made. He asks for a hearing before this kind of legislation is passed.
The idea expressed by the governor of the Bank of Canada, which is the idea we have expressed in this house, is a sound one and embodying this idea-and this might have been done at this time to avoid this kind of unhappy crisis in the future-the bank of England act reads, and I quote section 4(1):
The treasury may from time to time give such directions to the bank as, after consultation with the governor of the bank, they think necessary in the public interest.
Does the minister accept that as the responsibility of the government? He does not; the Secretary of State does.
Section 4(2) reads:
Subject to any such directions, the affairs of the bank shall be managed by the board of directors in accordance with such provisions (if any) in that behalf as may be continued in any charter of the bank for the time being in force and any bylaws made thereunder.
Instead of that kind of approach to this situation, when the government by its policy and by its tactics made such a situation inevitable, the government preferred to bring in the kind of bill we have before us. They preferred to declare this office vacant, by this bill and to discharge a high public official who holds office not at pleasure. I heard the hon. member for Carleton this afternoon try to assimilate the position of the governor of the Bank of Canada with a military officer who might be discharged in wartime. Of all the fantastic comparisons that probably is

the most ridiculous that has been made in this house for many years. No doubt he brought that particular military officer into his argument because that officer ran once as a Liberal candidate. But the idea that a public official such as the governor of the Bank of Canada holding his office on good behaviour should be assimilated to a military officer who should be discharged if he defaults in his duty in wartime, not by parliament but by the army or by the Department of National Defence, is just as ridiculous as the idea that a civil servant who has a protection, who has an appeal against injustice on dismissal should be assimilated with an official such as the governor of the Bank of Canada who holds his office on good behaviour, just as a judge holds his office on good behaviour and not as a deputy minister who holds his office at pleasure.
If you are to discharge by act of parliament as we are doing in this bill an official like the governor who holds his office on good behaviour, surely, Mr. Chairman, there must be evidence of misconduct to justify this kind of parliamentary action and the man who is charged with misconduct must surely be given a chance to defend himself before a committee of the parliament which is being asked to throw him out of his job. That is simple, elementary justice, and that is the issue in this bill. That justice has been denied to the governor whose office is being vacated by this bill and it is being denied without evidence having been brought forward to support the government's contention that there has been a fundamental difference of opinion between the governor and the government over all these years, a fundamental difference of policy discovered in the last month or two by the Minister of Finance who over the years before had been defending this governor against criticism from this side.
The Minister of Finance said in this house on February 21, as found at page 2266 of Hansard:
Since this government came into office there has never been the slightest interference with the bank's monetary policy.
This afternoon we heard the hon. member for Carleton say that over all these years the governor of the bank has been frustrating the economic, fiscal and other policies of the government, including monetary policies, and in spite of all that the Minister of Finance says, "Since this government came into office there has never been the slightest interference with the bank's monetary policy". Why this sudden interference on May 30 to the extent of asking the governor of the bank to resign without an opportunity to appear before a committee of the House of
Governor of Bank of Canada Commons which is being asked by legislation to throw him out of his job?
On February 21, 1961, the minister said in the same debate, as found at page 2257 of Hansard, that the government's position regarding the Bank of Canada is comparable to that with regard to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and that the government must keep its hands off the latter. That was the minister's doctrine of non-interference until May 30, 1961. What happened then? We hope during this committee hearing to have some light thrown on what happened then. We were told again this afternoon that it was a question of irreconcilability in regard to questions of fiscal and monetary policies. We did not hear anything about this until the last two or three weeks, and in the charges which have been levelled by the minister in the last two or three weeks against the governor of the Bank of Canada, charges which we asked to be brought before a committee of this house so that all parties could deal with them, and some of which were mentioned this afternoon, there is one major and specific charge levelled by the minister against the governor of the bank which might, if it could be substantiated, justify the government in asking for the governor's resignation. Here is the charge that was made by the Minister of Finance the other day:
That request-
This was the request made in 1957-58.
-which was designed by the government to ease tight money-
This is an important charge, an important accusation.
-was rejected by the governor firmly and angrily.
Let the minister, before this committee hearing is over, give us some evidence to support those words because we have no evidence. He has given us no evidence yet. On the contrary, on February 14, 1958, this was denied by the minister. I put these words on Hansard the other day and they bear repeating in respect of this one concrete, serious charge that the governor of the Bank of Canada rejected firmly and angrily a request from the government designed to ease tight money. On that point the Minister of Finance had this to say on February 14, 1958:
Money Is more plentiful, credit is somewhat easier and interest rates have been reduced to a remarkable extent in recent months.
Let the minister reconcile that statement with his charges levelled against the governor of the Bank of Canada, the main charge in his indictment which asks the House of Commons, because of that major charge, to pass an act of parliament, without referring
7514	HOUSE OF
Governor of Bank of Canada it to a committee, to throw the governor of the Bank of Canada out of his job.
Then there is the general charge which the minister repeated so often, and I quote it from page 6314 of Hansard, that the governor had "a rigid attitude on the maintenance of high interest rates". The minister has spent a lot of time in this house defending the governor and defending the government against our charge that there were high interest rates and trying to prove as recently as last February that those interest rates were lower than comparable rates in the United States and in the United Kingdom. Now he accuses the governor of the Bank of Canada of a rigid attitude on the maintenance of high interest rates.
Then, of course, we come to another clause in the indictment which has brought this bill before us, that the governor made speeches. That has been dealt with pretty effectively this afternoon. I will come back to the speeches a little later.
As far as interest rates are concerned, the minister said in February of this year, as found at page 2267 of Hansard, in an effort to exonerate the government and, indeed, to exonerate the governor from this charge of high interest rates:
Interest rates are determined... in this free economy in the light of thousands of transactions. It is a matter of the operation of the forces of supply and demand within quite limited statutory restrictions.
When the minister was specifically asked by the hon. member for Welland a couple of weeks ago, as found at page 6812 of Hansard, whether he had ever asked the governor to increase the money supply or to reduce interest rates he refused to reply. He said that was confidential information. We must not be told anything about that. Perhaps he will say something about that tonight.
We have also not only the minister's silence on this matter, not only the minister's contradiction of himself on this matter, but we have this sweeping denial of these charges by the governor in his statement of June 15 in which he said:
I repeat again that at no time has the Minister of Finance criticized or expressed a difference of opinion with the monetary policy being pursued by the Bank of Canada which, the bank and its board of directors were entitled to assume, carried the tacit approval of the government.
Over all these years the governor of the bank and the directors of the bank carried on and the only criticism the bank received on its monetary policy was from this side. The minister defended the bank and the bank had every right to assume that its policy was in consonance with the policy of the government. Then suddenly on May 30 the governor has to resign.


If the Minister of Finance now states that Mr. Coyne would not follow expansionist money policies, that he would not follow the expansionist money policies of this recent budget which provided for $65 million of tax reduction for expansion, how does he explain his statement on February 21 as found at page 2265 of Hansard? These are all questions which I expect the minister to deal with in the course of this committee discussion. How does he explain his statement on that date about the increase of the money supply in 1960 over 1959? How does he explain this statement, as recorded at page 2266 of Hansard for February 21, 1961:
The figure at December 31, 1960, is by far the largest on record and it is 5.5 per cent higher than the corresponding figure at the end of 1959.
Was the minister sincere? Was he telling the truth when he made that statement? If so, that means there was no disagreement between the governor and the government on the level of the money supply at least until February 21, 1961. What happened after that time? When the minister, according to his remarks reported at page 2267 of Hansard, defended the adequacy of interest rates and said that they were lower in Canada than in the United Kingdom and close to those of the United States, was he sincere? Was he telling the truth? If so, Mr. Chairman, there was no disagreement between the government and the governor on interest rates until after February 21, 1961.
When the minister, at page 2268, denied that the Bank of Canada had subordinated monetary policy to the interest of debt management, and when he defended the debt management policy of the government, including the conversion loan, was he sincere then? Was he telling the truth? If the answer is yes, then there was no disagreement between the government and the governor on the relations between debt management and monetary policy or on debt management policy itself. All of these things were fine in February of this year when we debated this matter. What has happened since that time to make the minister so drastically change his mind in regard to the policy of the governor of the bank that he had to throw him out of his job by an act of parliament without giving the governor a chance to be heard by a committee of this house?
When the Minister of Finance said a little earlier last year, on March 31, 1960, as reported at page 2673 of Hansard, that to contain inflationary pressures the government had reduced its borrowings and held a firm check on the expansion of government expenditures, was that in opposition to Mr. JULY 4, 1961
Coyne's views? Did the government disapprove of the fact that the bank increased the money supply between April and October, 1958 to help the conversion loan?
Then, Mr. Chairman, leaving the minister for a moment, to expose the hollow hypocrisy of this present attack on the governor, let us look at the Prime Minister's remarks on the "Nation's Business" on October 8, 1959, at a time when hon. gentlemen opposite tell us now the difference between the governor and the government had become irreconcilable. Having stated at that time that the economic climate had changed from one of recession to one of dynamic recovery, phenomenal economic recovery, the Prime Minister went on to say that this made money harder and more costly than heretofore; that interest rates had materially increased because the commercial banks had restricted their lending operations. Did he blame this on the governor of the bank or Bank of Canada? He blamed it then on the commercial banks.
Then, the Prime Minister went on to say:
In the first year after the government took office, there was a significant increase in the money supply in Canada. We were fighting recession.
This was the very year, that first year after he took office, that the Minister of Finance now tries to tell us he asked the governor of the Bank of Canada to increase the money supply and was firmly and angrily rejected by the governor of the bank. This is the main clause in his indictment against this governor whom he would now throw out of office without a chance of being heard before the banking and commerce committee of this house so that the governor could give his version of some of these statements.
The Prime Minister went on, in boasting about what the government had done to fight the recession by increasing the money supply, to say that it is the Bank of Canada, not the government that controls the money supply in Canada. From the end of June, 1957 until October 1, 1959, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance boasted that the money supply in chartered bank accounts had gone up from $11.5 billion to $13 billion and that in the past year the money supply had remained comparatively stable as a bulwark against inflation. Does that look as though the government were opposed to the policy of the Bank of Canada? The whole thing, Mr. Chairman, is arrant hypocrisy got together these last few weeks to buttress a case levelled against the governor of the Bank of Canada for some other reason, and to conceal the government's own confusion and their own ineptitude in the face of economic problems that were mounting.
There is no misconduct that can be levelled against the governor of the Bank of Canada
Governor of Bank of Canada who can be removed only for misconduct in monetary policy. Has there been any misconduct in what he has been saying in the last few years? If so would that justify his removal from office? Well, there was a meeting between the governor and the minister on March 18. We have heard quite a bit about that. At that meeting I believe the deputy minister of finance was present. I should like to ask the minister

and no doubt he will give us the information when he comes to reply to these questions-what were the subjects discussed during this meeting, other than the public speeches made by the governor? We know that the public speeches made by the governor were discussed. I ask the minister, did he personally object at that time to these speeches or did he make representations on behalf of his colleagues? What were those representations, and was this the first occasion, in March, 1961, that the Minister of Finance, either on his own behalf or on behalf of his colleagues, took exception to the speeches made by the governor of the Bank of Canada?
At page 6352 of Hansard for June 14, the minister is reported as saying:
I have been told by certain members of the board of directors of the Bank of Canada, to whom the governor is in a certain sense responsible, that some of them had given him warnings about these speeches.
I wonder if the minister would mind elaborating on that a little bit? He had been told by some directors that they had been warning the governor about his speeches. In March, then, he told the governor to make no more speeches of this kind, after the governor had been speaking for some years on these subjects and certainly since 1959 and at a time when those speeches were questioned in this House of Commons by the opposition and not a word of criticism came from the government. There was nothing but a defence of the right of this man to make these speeches. Now, the minister has the effrontery to put this forward as one of the reasons why the governor should be thrown out of his job without a chance to be heard in his own defence before a committee of this house.
When the minister defended the right of the governor to make public speeches, as he did in February of this year, on the ground that Mr. Coyne was a citizen of a free country and the minister had no right of censorship, was the minister sincere at that time? Was he telling us the truth? If he was, Mr. Chairman, that means that until February 21, 1961 at least, the governor's speeches were not an issue. Why did they become an issue after February 21? Since on February 21, 1961 the minister had told the house he had
7516	HOUSE OF
Governor of Bank of Canada no right of censorship over the speeches of the governor of the Bank of Canada, when and why did he change his mind about this right of censorship which he repudiated a few short months ago? Since the minister now claims he had been for a long time of the opinion that these speeches were putting the government in an embarrassing position and that the bank was becoming a centre of political controversy, why did the minister wait until March, 1961 to raise the issue with the governor?
Having raised the issue on March 18, did the governor agree to remain silent and not make any more speeches? When the governor acepted the minister's request on March 18, could the minister expect from the governor any more than that? Did he not feel that the issue had been satisfactorily settled? If so, why did he drag it up on May 30 along with the pension? There are a good many other things we want to bring up in this committee discussion, Mr. Chairman. One is the relationship of the directors, not only to the governor over this issue but the relationship of the directors to the minister, and the contact that they had with the minister. It is quite clear that all contacts, and all communications, effective consultation and communication between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the minister, had disappeared over the years. I admit that it was an impossible arrangement. However, I believe that the minister had more to do with that responsibility and with that negative relationship, than had the governor himself.
But while that relationship did not exist between the governor and the minister, apparently a very close relationship existed between some of the directors of the board and the minister and perhaps the minister will explain that kind of relationship. But that kind of relationship was not close enough, so we are told now by the minister, to inform the minister that this Tory board of directors voted an increased pension to the governor of the Bank of Canada in February, 1960.
Under a pension committee headed by Mr. Bryden who had been working on this subject for a long time or for some months, this Tory subcommittee and this Tory board voted this increased pension to the governor of the Bank of Canada in February, 1960. Yet the minister now tells us he heard nothing about it until the spring of 1961. That is a shocking state of affairs. The assistant deputy minister was at the meeting of the board when the pensions were increased by this Tory board of directors. The deputy minister was at the next meeting when the minutes of the previous meeting were read out. The assistant deputy minister knew about it. The deputy


minister knew about it. But the minister tells us he did not know about it.

I was asked in the first place by the Leader of the Opposition why this bill had not been brought forward as an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act. I should have thought the reason was obvious. This is a bill brought forward for a particular purpose. It is not continuing legislation. It is not the kind of legislation which purports to have continuing effects in the future. Therefore it was deemed appropriate, in the light of the best legislative counsel available, to bring forward this measure as a separate bill, having regard to the fact that it has an immediate purpose.
As to the questions concerning such a situation in the future or other situations to which the present circumstances may give rise, I have already on another occasion

Governor of Bank of Canada announced that the government will shortly be appointing a royal commission to study all questions relating to banking, including the Bank of Canada, credit, money and other questions in this country, and it will be within the purview of that royal commission to examine all questions in relation to the operation of the Bank of Canada which bear upon the need for any legislative change in the terms of that act.
Some of the questions asked tonight are obviously questions which I am precluded from answering in the way in which some of them were asked without divulging communications which are of a confidential nature. We have already faced this question with regard to several of the motions put forward by hon. members opposite for production of papers of interest at various stages of this subject. The house has reaffirmed the principle in relation to those motions that where communications are of a confidential nature, as are communications passing between the Minister of Finance on the one hand and the governor of the Bank of Canada on the other, that confidence must be preserved. I must respect the decision of the house in that regard. It would be very tempting indeed to follow the governor of the Bank of Canada in the course he has taken. He has felt himself at liberty to forget and ignore the confidential nature of some of the communications, which he has, without any leave whatever and in a very improper manner, made public.
I do not intend to follow that improper and irresponsible course. Communications which are confidential must have their confidential nature respected. The governor has chosen to make public certain things in those communications which he considers, evidently, might be of advantage to him. Perhaps there are communications which have passed between us which, for equal reasons, I might find it to my advantage and to the advantage of the government to make public in that way. But there is a principle involved here which must be respected not only for its intrinsic merit in this situation but for the sake of all future relationships between confidential advisers of the government and ministers of the crown.
Let me turn briefly in this regard to the question put by the hon. member for Burn-aby-Coquitlam, because here is an example. That hon. member asked me specifically to disclose the advice given by Mr. Coyne to the government in relation to certain questions of debt management with respect to the money-raising program for the present year. It would be highly improper on my part to disclose advice given to me or to the government by the adviser in this respect,


which is the Bank of Canada. I have to say that in this field of debt management the government takes its responsibility. I made that very clear when I spoke in this house on June 26. In the field of debt management, the Bank of Canada acts as adviser to the government. The government will take its responsibility for whatever advice it takes from its adviser and acts upon, or whatever advice it does not take and does not act upon. This is the responsibility of the government and that responsibility will be discharged. It would be very unfair either to the adviser in this particular case or the advisers of the government in other cases if ministers were to disclose in the house advice of a very confidential nature given to them in this regard.

I had entertained the opinion when in opposition, and had so expressed myself in debate, that there was a responsibility on the part of the government in the field of monetary policy. Hon. members opposite have quoted what I said in this respect in a debate in the house in 1956. That was an opinion which I certainly held at that time. Governor of Bank of Canada when we were in opposition. Then I proceeded, Mr. Chairman, as reported at page 7040 of Hansard for June 26, 1961:

I told him it was from the government, Mr. Chairman. I have to tell you again that that request of the government was rejected firmly, yes, and angrily. It was made very clear, Mr. Chairman, and what has happened since in relation to monetary policy and what I have said since in this house in relation to monetary policy, has to be seen in that setting. It was made very clear to me in that meeting that the governor of the Bank of Canada felt quite free to reject requests of the government in relation to monetary measures. This was made very clear to me.
As I said speaking in the house on June 26, this brought me up pretty short, to be told firmly, flatly and angrily that this request from the government was rejected.

I had to come to the conclusion, after an exhaustive study of the statute, that parliament had not given to the government authority over the Bank of Canada in relation to the question of money supply. I have drawn attention in this house during various debates to the terms of the Bank of Canada Act which give to the Bank of Canada and to the Bank of Canada alone the power to create money in Canada. Questions of money supply, therefore, are under the Bank of Canada.
Here was the situation from that point on. As I pointed out in speaking in this House of Commons on June 26, from that point on the governor of the Bank of Canada and other authorities in the bank were always ready to discuss monetary policy. They were always prepared to explain it and to defend it. But, Mr. Chairman, the stage had been set at the very beginning in this meeting of 1957-58. I have told the house frankly that in this situation we had to consider whether we would try to force the issue at that time, and we decided that we would try to live with this situation until December 31, 1961. I pointed out that we had co-operation from the bank authorities in the field of debt management, the servicing of the public debt and these other matters on which the bank acts as adviser. But, Mr. Chairman, in relation to monetary policy the relationship was established in that meeting in 1957-58 or towards the end of 1957 and that is the way in which the matter rested.
If we had been able to look into some crystal ball and had seen that we would be faced in the spring and early summer of 1961 with the situation which has now arisen, obviously we would not have waited. If we were going to have an issue like this raised in parliament, it would have been better had it been raised earlier. However, we thought this situation could be lived with and we were concerned, above all other things, that no harm should be done to the Bank of Canada because of its importance as a national institution.

Not at all. I am asked to make comment on this question. It brings one back to the question of responsibility in relation to monetary policy. I am sorry that the hon. member for Laurier thinks I did not deal with his question earlier. I thought I was dealing with it when I made comment on this matter of authority in this field.
The fact is-and here I am coming back to what I said in my report to the house on June 26-that if you have under the existing system, under the existing act, someone at the bank directing the affairs of the bank who is co-operative, then I suppose you can have, under the existing system and under the existing statute, the same kind of effective cooperation that you had when Mr. Graham Towers was governor of the bank.
These questions about the relative areas of responsibility, fiscal on the one hand and monetary on the other, did not arise in the days of Mr. Graham Towers' governorship except in an academic sense. He came to the banking and commerce committee on one occasion. My esteemed friend, the hon. member for Greenwood, asked him questions on this subject, but everyone knew that these were academic questions because there had been no situation in which the friction had arisen; in which there was lack of co-operation between the authorities in the fiscal field and the authorities in the monetary field.

Governor of Bank of Canada
It is only when you have a situation such as we have, to my very great regret, under the existing governor that you are thrown back on the provisions that parliament has written in the statute. The fact is that where you do not get co-operation; where you do not get people working together; where you do not get the effective meshing together of fiscal policy and monetary policy, then the Bank of Canada Act in its terms today does not give the government authority in this field. It gives the government power to appoint the governor, but not to remove him. It gives the government power to appoint directors, but not to remove them. I pointed this out in the debate in this house on February 22 last.
Hon. members opposite were told these things very plainly and the Leader of the Opposition and I had a debate on this subject. But there is the situation. If we are to be governed by the terms of the statute, then there is the situation where the government has no authority to impose, under the present system, its will on the Bank of Canada in relation to monetary policy.

We had to recognize these limitations on the authority of the government and hope that in due time there would be an opportunity to effect an improvement in that regard. I am quite sure that an improvement will be coming if parliament sees fit to adopt this present measure.

maintopic: C.N.R. GRANTS IN LIEU OF TAX, HALIFAX
speechtext:
1.	Does the Canadian National Railways pay grants to the city of Halifax in lieu of taxation on Canadian National Railways property?
2.	If so, what is the formula used in the payment of such grants, and is the formula related to the so-called commercial tax rate or to the residential tax rate applied by the city of Halifax to taxpayers?
3.	What was the total grant paid by the Canadian National Railways to the city of Halifax in lieu of taxation on Canadian National Railways properties in (a) 1956 (b) 1957 (c) 1958 (d) 1959 (e) 1960?
4.	What was the total accepted value of Canadian National Railways properties on which the 1960 grant to the city of Halifax was based, what portion represented land, and what portion represented buildings?
Answer by: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of
Transport):
The management of Canadian National Railways advise as follows:
1.	Yes.
Question
2.	Valuation: Railway roadway, according to average value of adjoining lands. Land, other than roadway, at actual value. Buildings, stations, freight sheds, offices, warehouses, elevators, hotels, roundhouses and machine repair and other shops at actual value.
Rate: 50 per cent of the merged average rate of taxation for the five year period immediately preceding the commencement year of the agreement. "Merged rate"-means the effective rate if the residential and commercial rates were not operative.
Note: Land and buildings thereon, under lease are excluded from the grant. Valuations are revised annually to allow for changes in holdings and leaseholds.
